text: Metrics are numbers over time; a log is a detailed, often unstructured record of an event — a web server access line, an application error with a stack trace, an operating-system message. CloudWatch Logs is the centralized, searchable store those records land in, retained there long after the instance that produced them might be gone — a genuinely separate piece of the CloudWatch umbrella from the metrics and alarms covered so far.

Every log reaching CloudWatch lives under two levels of organization. A log group is the top-level container, typically one per application or resource — a custom group like /ec2/web01/var-log-messages for an instance's system log. Inside it, a log stream is a sequence of events from one specific source, like one instance or one Lambda invocation. Retention is set per group, defaulting to Never Expire but commonly set to 30, 90, or 365 days instead.

Platform metrics come from the hypervisor, which can't see inside the guest OS — that's why memory usage never shows up automatically. The exact same limitation hits logs: a file like /var/log/messages sitting on an instance's own disk never reaches CloudWatch Logs by itself. Something running inside the OS has to ship it there.

That something is the CloudWatch Agent, installed on the instance and driven by a config file listing which local log files to watch and which log group to send each one to. The same agent can also push custom OS-level metrics, including memory and disk usage, closing the exact gap Lesson 21 flagged.

Once log data is flowing, CloudWatch Logs Insights is the query language for searching it, piped top to bottom much like the Azure course's KQL — filtering every log stream in a group for ERROR lines at once, instead of SSHing into each instance by hand to check. Next, Lesson 24 covers a record that neither metrics nor logs can provide: who actually did something to an AWS resource, and when.
